2245.t: Related to ἥδομαι (hḗdomai, “to rejoice”) and ἡδύς (hēdŭ́s, “sweet”).

2217.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰl̥h₃rós Proto-Hellenic *kʰlōrós Ancient Greek χλωρός From Proto-Hellenic *kʰlōrós, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-.

2255.t: Phono-semantic matching of Latin Rōma with ῥώμη (rhṓmē, “power, strength, might"”).

2280.t: From the stem of λέπω (lépō, “to peel”) + -ρός (-rós).

2260.t: From Old Persian 𐏂𐎢𐏁𐎠 (ç-u-š-a /⁠Çūšā⁠/), from Elamite 𒀸𒋗𒊺𒂗 (Šušen).

2275.t: From Proto-Indo-European *dʰers-. Cognates include Sanskrit धृष्णोति (dhṛṣṇóti), Czech drzý and Lithuanian drąsus.

2298.t: Probably from earlier πραΰς (prāŭ̈́s) (through the adverb πράως (práōs), contracted from πραέως (praéōs)), which can be regularly derived from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂-i-w-, but the traditional comparison with what is now reconstructed as *preyH- (“to…

2267.t: Unclear. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gong-; compare Sanskrit गङ्गूयति (gaṅgūyati, “to shout”) and गुञ्जति (guñjati, “to buzz, purr, hum”).

2215.t: From φυτός (phŭtós, “natural; which has grown naturally”), from φύω (phúō, “to generate; cause to grow”).

2269.t: From Proto-Indo-European *dweynós, from *dwey- (“fear”); equivalent to δει- (dei-), the root of δείδω (deídō), + -νος (-nos). Compare δέος (déos).

2216.t: Same source as φυλάσσω (phŭlắssō, “to guard; to watch”), but of unknown further etymology. According to Beekes, both words are clear examples of Pre-Greek.

2284.t: According to Beekes, a back-formation from μελετάω (meletáō). Connected with μέλω (mélō).

2213.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷʰtʰéřřō, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰér-ye-ti, from *dʰgʷʰer- (“flow, diverge; perish”) via the middle form φθείρομαι (phtheíromai, “to be destroyed, perish”) with new active meaning “destroy”.

2214.t: From φροντίς (phrontís, “thought”) + *-ϳω (*-jō), superficially containing -ίζω (-ízō). Related to φρήν (phrḗn).

2200.t: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *p(y)eh₂w- (“to strike, hit”), and cognate with Latin paviō (“to beat, strike”) and Lithuanian pjáuti (“to reap, cut”).

2278.t: κτίζω (ktĭ́zō, “found, build”) + -σις (-sĭs). Cognate with Sanskrit क्षितिज (kṣitija).

2266.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gʷā́mə, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷéh₂mn̥, from *gʷeh₂- (“to step”) (whence ἔβην (ébēn)). Compare βωμός (bōmós, “altar”).

2218.t: Related to χρῶμα (khrôma), of uncertain origin. According to Beekes, probably cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀒𐀫𐀸𐀁 (a-ko-ro-we-e) (representing either /akʰroweʰe/ [dual noun] “without spots”, or /ha-kʰroweʰe/ “of one color”).

2296.t: From προαιρέομαι (proairéomai) + -σις (-sis). From προ- (pro-) + αἵρεσις (haíresis, “taking; choice”).

2241.t: Denominative of ἐτός (etós, “true”), i.e. "to verify, check the truth of" > "to examine, test".

2204.t: From στάξ (stắx, “drop”) + *-ϳω (*-jō), of uncertain origin; also found in σταγών (stăgṓn, “drop”).

2225.t: Unknown. The variant points to foreign or Pre-Greek origin.

2229.t: According to Beekes, from ἁβρός (habrós, “delicate, graceful”).

2299.t: From Proto-Indo-European *pṓds, like πέδον (pédon) and πέζα (péza). The same semantics are found in Latin pedica (“shackle”), impediō (“to hinder”) and Proto-Germanic *feturaz (“fetter”).

2273.t: From εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + γένος (génos, “birth, offspring, stock”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix) from γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “become”). Compare Εὐγένιος (Eugénios).

2248.t: From ὀκνέω (oknéō, “to shrink, hesitate”) + -ρός (-rós, adjective suffix).

2287.t: Formed from νέος (néos, “new”), probably after the example of περισσός (perissós, “extraordinary, prodigious”), ἔπισσαι (épissai) or μέτασσαι (métassai).

2219.t: Analyzed by Fick as a univerbation from the aorist form of ψάλλω (psállō, “to pluck, pull, twitch”) (the ultimate source of psalm) and ἀφάω (apháō, “to handle”). It remains unclear, however, why the aorist was preferred.

2263.t: From αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) + χθών (khthṓn, “earth, soil”), sprung from the land itself.

2274.t: Univerbation of εὖ (eû, “well”) + γε (ge, emphatic particle).

2239.t: According to Beekes, a denominative from *ἐρεϝ-(ε)ν- (*erew-(e)n-), a noun itself derived from earlier *ἐρεϝω (*erewō), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rew-.
